title: Write each avatar as a job in a situation, not a demographic label
hypothesis: If we replace demographic labels with a specific job and circumstance, then copy and creative get sharper because they aim at real motivation instead of a description.

signal.check: Avatar docs lead with age, gender or income and have no sentence describing what the customer is trying to get done.

risk.note: None. This only changes how the avatar is written, not any live asset.

prerequisites: A brand record with the product and any reviews or customer notes
steps: Pull the reviews, tickets, or notes that describe why people buy.
Write one sentence: what the customer is trying to get done, and in what situation.
Move age, gender, and income into a background section, not the top line.
Reject any avatar draft that has only demographic fields.
Rewrite one old brief that leads with a demographic as a test.

test.method: Run 2 versions of a hook or PDP line, one built from the job statement and one from a demographic label.
test.read_point: After the store's normal test spend or sample size.

title: Record the functional, emotional and social side of every job
hypothesis: If we write all 3 sides of a job, functional, emotional and social, instead of only the functional one, then copy can use the angle that most moves this avatar.
does_not_apply_when: Purchase has no real emotional or social weight, such as a pure commodity repurchase

signal.check: Avatar record only lists a functional benefit, with no emotional or social line.

prerequisites: A job statement for the avatar
steps: For the job statement, write the functional result in one line.
Write the emotional payoff in one line, how they will feel.
Write the social payoff in one line, what others will think or see.
Mark any line 'no evidence yet' if reviews or interviews do not support it.
Use whichever line has the most quotes behind it as the lead angle.

test.method: Test a hook built on the emotional or social line against the current functional-only hook.

title: Split one buyer into two avatars when the circumstance changes the job
hypothesis: If research shows the same person buys for different situations, then splitting the avatar record by situation moves conversion because each version speaks to the real moment.
does_not_apply_when: Research shows only one situation drives the purchase

signal.check: Interviews or reviews show the same type of buyer purchasing for two different situations or goals.

risk.note: Splitting a record can be undone by merging it back if the evidence does not hold up.

prerequisites: At least 2 source quotes or interviews showing different situations for the same product
steps: Compare quotes across avatar candidates for the same product.
Check if the buying moment or goal differs, such as a morning use versus an evening use.
If they differ, write 2 separate avatar records instead of one averaged one.
Tag each record with its trigger situation so copy does not mix them.

test.method: Run creative built for each split avatar separately and compare against the old combined avatar's creative.
test.read_point: After normal test spend for each.

title: Rewrite generic need and attribute words into a specific job sentence
hypothesis: If we replace words like feel confident or premium with a specific verb plus noun job, then the record gives copy something testable instead of a mood word.

signal.check: The avatar record's job field is a need word (confident, healthy) or an attribute word (premium, eco-friendly) instead of a sentence.

prerequisites: A candidate need or attribute word from research
steps: Find the need or attribute word in the record.
Ask what specific circumstance and result it points to.
Rewrite it as verb plus noun describing progress.
Check the new sentence names no product, only progress.

test.method: Compare copy from the attribute word against copy from the rewritten job sentence.

title: Validate every job statement with the verb-noun test and the cross-category test
hypothesis: If every job statement passes the verb plus noun test and lists cross-category alternatives, then the avatar record stays testable instead of turning into a preference list.

signal.check: A job statement reads as an adjective list, or every alternative to it is a SKU in the same category.

risk.note: None, this is a writing check.

prerequisites: A draft job statement
steps: Write the job as verb plus noun describing progress.
Reject it if it is only adjectives, such as convenient or trustworthy.
List everything that could be hired for this job.
If every option is a SKU in the same category, go up one level of abstraction and rewrite.
Repeat until the alternatives span different categories, including doing nothing.
Check the 3 dimensions are present or marked no evidence yet.
Check a real struggle exists; if not, mark the job statement optional.

test.method: Have a second person read the job statement and list who or what it could lose to; if they can only name same-category products, send it back.

title: Re-check if the job moved before rewriting an avatar after a competitor launch
hypothesis: If we check whether the underlying job changed or only the solution changed when a competitor launches something new, then we avoid rewriting an avatar record that is still correct.
does_not_apply_when: No competitor or category shift has happened recently

signal.check: A competitor launched a new product or feature and the team wants to rewrite the avatar record because of it.

prerequisites: An existing avatar record
steps: When a competitor changes its product, ask what job the customer is still trying to do.
Check if new reviews or forum posts show a new job, or the same job with a new solution.
If the job is the same, keep the job statement and only note the new competing solution.
Only rewrite the job statement if fresh evidence shows the underlying job changed.

test.method: Compare old and new evidence quotes before and after the competitor change.
test.read_point: Within a month of the competitor change.

title: List the full competitive set for every avatar, including doing nothing
hypothesis: If the avatar record lists every real alternative including doing nothing and out-of-category options, then offer and copy can address the actual competition instead of only rival SKUs.

signal.check: The record's competitive set only lists direct competitor products, with no do-nothing or out-of-category option.

prerequisites: A validated job statement
steps: List direct competitor products for the job.
List workarounds and DIY options people use instead.
List doing nothing as an option and why some people choose it.
List any out-of-category product that competes for the same job.
Hand the do-nothing and out-of-category entries to the offer agent as objections to address.

test.method: Test copy or an offer angle that names the do-nothing option against copy that only names rival products.

title: Keep demographic fields as background context, never as the reason in copy
hypothesis: If demographic fields stay in a context block and never lead copy, then creative keeps aiming at the real job instead of drifting into a stereotype.

signal.check: A brief or ad script opens with an age, gender or income line instead of the job or trigger.

prerequisites: An avatar record with a job statement
steps: Move all demographic fields into a labeled context block at the bottom of the record.
Check every brief for lines that open with a demographic instead of the job or trigger.
Rewrite any such line to open with the situation instead.
Keep demographic data only for platform and placement decisions, not for copy.

test.method: Compare a hook that opens on demographics against one that opens on the job or trigger.

title: Mark low-stakes or impulse purchases as not needing a full job record
hypothesis: If we skip deep job research for a low-stakes, impulse or commodity repurchase and say so in the record, then research time goes to products where it actually changes copy.
does_not_apply_when: The product carries real functional, emotional or social weight for the buyer

signal.check: A cheap, low-stakes or habitual repurchase item shows no real struggle in reviews, tickets or interviews.

risk.note: If later evidence shows a real struggle, restart the job work.

prerequisites: Enough reviews or notes to judge stakes
steps: Check whether reviews, tickets or interviews show real frustration, fear or social stakes.
If none show up after a normal research pass, mark the job statement as optional in the record.
Keep any quotes collected even without a full job statement.
Spend the saved research time on a product or avatar with real struggle.

test.method: Track research hours spent on low-stakes items before and after applying this rule.

title: Use the feels-true-on-first-read check only to break a tie between 2 job statements
hypothesis: If the team uses whether a job statement feels obviously true, not whether it needs defending, as a soft tie-break between 2 candidates, then it avoids arguing itself into an unproven idea.
does_not_apply_when: Only 1 job statement candidate exists, or hard evidence already decides between them

signal.check: Two competing job statements exist and the team is debating which is right without new evidence.

risk.note: This is a soft check, never a final decision.

prerequisites: 2 candidate job statements from the same evidence set
steps: Read both job statements without discussion.
Note which one the team accepts immediately versus which one needs defending.
Treat the one needing defending as unproven, not wrong.
Gather more evidence, such as interviews or reviews, before picking either as final.

test.method: Track whether the statement chosen this way holds up after more evidence comes in.

title: Record push, pull, habit and anxiety for every avatar
hypothesis: If every avatar record names the push of the problem, the pull of the new option, the habit of the present, and the anxiety of switching, then copy and offer can target the force that is actually missing.

signal.check: The avatar record lists a desire or pain point but does not separate push, pull, habit and anxiety.

prerequisites: At least 1 interview or detailed review for this avatar
steps: From interviews or reviews, write one quote for the push, what got worse.
Write one quote for the pull, what attracted them to the new option.
Write one quote for the habit, what they were doing before, however bad.
Write one quote for the anxiety, what almost stopped them from switching.
Flag any force with no quote as no evidence yet and probe for it in the next interview.

test.method: Test copy that speaks to the weakest force, usually anxiety, against current copy.

title: Give the anxiety side of the record as much weight as the benefit side
hypothesis: If we spend as much effort writing and testing anxiety removers as we do writing benefits, then conversion improves, because loss aversion is roughly twice as strong as the pull of an equal gain.

signal.check: The record or brief lists several benefits but 1 or 0 anxieties with a real remover.

expected_effect.size: unknown, the cited loss aversion effect is about 2x an equal gain

prerequisites: The 4 forces field filled in
steps: Count the benefits and the anxieties currently written in the record.
For every benefit, add at least one anxiety with a real remover from evidence.
Route any anxiety with no remover yet to the offer and page agents to test, such as a guarantee or a review.
Weight test ideas so anxiety removal gets equal test slots to benefit messaging.

test.method: Test an anxiety removal message, such as a guarantee or proof point, against a benefit-only message at the same funnel step.

title: Name the exact thing the customer stopped using before they bought
hypothesis: If the record names the specific product, workaround or choice the customer fired, with its cost when known, then copy can speak directly to that switch instead of a vague competitor mention.

signal.check: The record's fired or failed-solution field is blank or says something generic like other products.

prerequisites: At least 1 quote naming a prior product or workaround
steps: Search reviews, tickets and interviews for phrases like I used to, I switched from, instead of.
Name the exact product, workaround, or the choice of doing nothing.
Note the cost and extent when given, such as a dollar amount or a time span.
Note what made that old choice untenable, in the customer's words.
Leave the field blank and flagged if no quote supports a specific fired alternative yet.

test.method: Test copy that names the specific fired alternative against generic switch-to-us copy.

title: Log the customer's current workaround as a competitor with no marketing budget
hypothesis: If we log a long-standing workaround as a real competitor and note why it persists, then the offer and copy can address the actual reason people stay stuck, not just rival brands.

signal.check: Research shows a workaround, such as adding water to food or a shoebox of receipts, that customers keep using despite its flaws.

prerequisites: A quote describing a long-standing workaround
steps: Find quotes describing a workaround the customer used for a long time.
Log it in the competitive set as a habit competitor, not a brand.
Write down why it persists, such as it's free or familiar or switching feels risky.
Hand this reason to the offer agent as an objection to remove.

test.method: Test copy or an offer that names the workaround and its downside against copy that ignores it.

title: Pair every objection with the real thing that removed it, not a guess
hypothesis: If every objection in the record is paired with what actually removed it in a real purchase, then the page and offer teams test proven removers instead of inventing reassurance copy.

signal.check: The record lists objections with no matching remover, or the remover is guessed rather than sourced from a real purchase or review.

prerequisites: At least 1 objection identified in research
steps: List every objection found in reviews, tickets or interviews.
For each, search for what removed it in a real case, such as a return policy or a proof point.
Mark any objection with no known remover as untested instead of inventing one.
Send untested objections to the offer and landing page agents to test a remover.

test.method: Test a page or offer element that removes a specific named objection against a version without it.

title: Treat repeat purchase or subscription retention as proof the avatar's job is solved
hypothesis: If we require repeat purchase or subscription retention data for an avatar before calling it confirmed, then the team stops crediting a good first sale as proof the underlying job is actually solved.

signal.check: An avatar is marked confirmed or successful based only on first-purchase or ad-click data, with no repeat purchase or retention check.

prerequisites: Repeat purchase rate or subscription retention data per SKU
steps: Pull repeat purchase rate or subscription retention for the SKU tied to this avatar.
Compare it against the store's overall repeat rate.
Mark the avatar provisional until repeat use or repeat purchase shows up for it specifically.
Only mark the avatar validated once the little-hire data confirms it.

test.method: Track repeat purchase rate for orders tagged to this avatar's angle over the next purchase window.
test.read_point: After 1 full repeat purchase cycle for the product.

title: Write emotional and social fields for B2B and gift-buyer avatars, not just a rational profile
hypothesis: If a B2B or gift-giving avatar record still includes emotional and social fields, then copy avoids a flat, purely rational pitch that misses the real decision driver.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has no B2B, wholesale or gifting line

signal.check: A B2B, wholesale or gift avatar record only lists functional or rational buying criteria.

prerequisites: A B2B, wholesale or gift-giving line identified in the brand record
steps: Identify any B2B, wholesale or gift-giving line in the brand.
Add an emotional field: what does this buyer fear looking like to others, such as unprepared or cheap.
Add a social field: who is watching this decision, such as a board, a spouse or a recipient.
Fold these into the job spec alongside the functional criteria.

test.method: Test copy or a sales page that names the emotional or social stake against a purely rational, feature-only version.
test.read_point: After normal test spend or sales cycle.

title: Build a separate churn record for subscription avatars, not just an acquisition record
hypothesis: If a subscription brand builds a churn or win-back record from lapsed-subscriber conversations, separate from the acquisition avatar, then it can find and fix a specific reason people cancel.
does_not_apply_when: The brand sells one-off purchases only

signal.check: The brand sells on subscription and has an acquisition avatar record but no record built from why subscribers cancel.

prerequisites: A subscription business model
Access to lapsed subscriber contacts
steps: Pull a list of recently lapsed or cancelled subscribers.
Run loss conversations asking directly why they left.
Log fixable reasons separately from the acquisition avatar's record.
Hand fixable reasons to the retention or support team as a specific fix, such as a support gap.
Track whether the fix changes subscription churn for that segment.

test.method: After a fix from a churn record, such as adding live chat, track subscription churn for the same cohort.
test.read_point: 1 to 2 billing cycles after the fix.

title: Run all 5 discovery lenses to find avatar candidates a feature survey would miss
hypothesis: If we run 5 separate discovery passes, own life, nonconsumption, workarounds, negative jobs and unusual uses, instead of one general research pass, then we surface avatar candidates that a single survey or forum read would miss.

signal.check: The brand has only run one type of research pass, such as reviews only, and has not looked at cart abandoners, workarounds, or unusual product uses.

prerequisites: A research evidence file for the brand
steps: Own life: log any personal or team experience with the product's problem, with a real quote if possible.
Nonconsumption: pull cart abandoners and category non-buyers and note why they did not buy.
Workarounds: pull support tickets and reviews describing a jury-rigged use.
Negative jobs: look for checkout dread or friction people mention avoiding.
Unusual uses: mine reviews and UGC for uses the brand did not design for.
Log a verbatim quote and trigger circumstance for each candidate found, not an inferred need.

test.method: Compare the number and quality of candidates found across all 5 lenses against a single-lens pass.

title: Anchor the avatar on top customers if the brand has buyers, or competitor ads if it has none
hypothesis: If we anchor the avatar on the brand's own top customers when buyers exist, and on competitor ads and reviews only when they do not, then the record starts from the strongest evidence available instead of a guess.

signal.check: The brand has existing customers with order history, or it is a pre-launch or new-market product with none.

risk.note: A record anchored on competitor data alone should stay marked provisional.

prerequisites: A customer list with a value ranking for an existing brand, or Ad Library access for a new one
steps: Check if the brand has an existing customer list.
If yes, rank customers by revenue, margin or repeat count and pull the top cut for interviews and review mining.
If no, run the Ad Library map and mine competitor and marketplace reviews instead.
Mark any record built without first-party buyers as provisional until real buyers confirm it.

test.method: Compare conversion on creative built from the top-customer anchor against creative built from a general or competitor-based guess.

title: Scan reviews for identity markers like I am a or As a to find avatar candidates
hypothesis: If we pull reviews for repeated self-descriptions like I am a nurse or As a new mom, then we find real avatar candidates that a feature-based read of reviews would miss.

signal.check: Reviews have not been scanned specifically for self-description phrases across the brand's own, competitor, and generic marketplace listings.

prerequisites: Access to the brand's own reviews, competitor reviews, and one high-review generic listing
steps: Search reviews for phrases like I am a, As a, and similar self-descriptions.
Pull from 3 places: the brand's own reviews, competitor reviews, and a generic high-review listing.
Tally how often each identity marker repeats across independent reviews.
Treat a marker that repeats across independent reviews as a candidate; 1 mention is not enough.

test.method: Compare candidate quality found through identity-marker scanning against the brand's current avatar guesses.

title: Require a pattern across independent sources before an avatar candidate counts
hypothesis: If no candidate enters the priority list on 1 quote, 1 review or 1 call, then the priority list holds real, repeating patterns instead of dramatic one-off stories.

signal.check: A candidate avatar or angle is being considered based on a single striking quote, review, or call.

prerequisites: A running evidence file with quote counts by theme
steps: Before adding a candidate to the priority list, count how many independent sources show the same theme.
Reject a candidate resting on 1 quote, 1 review, or 1 call.
Keep collecting evidence for a promising single quote instead of acting on it.
Once a pattern holds, go one level deeper, for example not just ecom owners but ecom owners over 100k a month.

test.method: Track how many candidates rejected on this rule later reappeared with a real pattern versus never resurfaced.

title: Watch for the category splitting into sub-avatars as buyers get more sophisticated
hypothesis: If we track how a category is splitting into sub-avatars, such as a general audience breaking into specific sub-groups, then we can find an underserved slice before it saturates.
does_not_apply_when: The category is still in a generic just sell it to me stage, with no sign of buyer sophistication

signal.check: The category shows early signs of splitting, such as competitors starting to target a narrower slice than the mass market.

risk.note: Named brand characterizations may be out of date; re-check before reuse.

prerequisites: A view of the category's main competitors and their positioning
steps: List the category's mass-market players and their generic pitch.
Look for brands that have already split off a narrower slice, such as by identity, use case, or life stage.
Map the layers: mass layer, niche layer, sub-avatar layer.
Identify the next unserved slice within that structure.
Check the size of that slice before committing (see the niche size check).

test.method: Run a small test campaign aimed at the identified sub-avatar and compare cost per result against the mass-market campaign.

title: Check the parent market and sub-niche are big enough before committing to a narrow avatar
hypothesis: If we estimate the parent market and sub-niche size before locking a very narrow avatar, then we avoid building a whole creative and offer strategy around a segment too small to promote into.

signal.check: A very narrow avatar is being proposed with no estimate of how many people fit it.

risk.note: A wrong size estimate can send the team after too small an audience; treat the estimate as rough.

prerequisites: Access to keyword volume tools or subreddit membership counts
steps: Estimate the parent market size using a rough figure (industry size, subreddit or forum size).
Estimate the sub-niche size within it using thread volume, subreddit membership, or keyword search volume.
Log the basis for both estimates in the record.
If the sub-niche looks too small to promote into, widen the avatar or pick a different candidate.

test.method: Run a small paid test at the estimated audience size and check if it can spend a normal daily budget without exhausting reach.
test.read_point: After a few days of a small test budget.

title: Audit the product's real mechanism before deciding to differentiate by avatar instead
hypothesis: If we check whether the product has a real visual, mechanical or functional difference before leaning on avatar work, then we route genuinely different products to product and offer work instead of over-relying on niching.

signal.check: The product looks like a commodity or an AliExpress-style item with no clear checked difference from competitors.

risk.note: Never claim a mechanism the product does not have.

prerequisites: A clear view of the product and its closest competitors
steps: Compare the product against its closest competitors on visual, mechanical, and functional grounds.
Write down any real, provable difference found.
If a real difference exists, route the product to product research and offer work, and use avatar work only for the messaging layer.
If no real difference exists, treat a very specific avatar as the main lever for this product.

test.method: No test needed; this is a routing decision made before committing research time.
test.read_point: Before starting a new avatar research cycle.

title: Map the mainstream avatar in the Meta Ad Library before building a new one
hypothesis: If we map who competitors already speak to in the Ad Library before picking a new avatar, then the new avatar clearly avoids the crowded profile instead of accidentally repeating it.
does_not_apply_when: Few competitors run ads in this category

signal.check: The category has active advertisers in the Meta Ad Library and no one has mapped who they target yet.

risk.note: This is a read of competitor creative choices, not measured audience data; label any age or gender read as an estimate.

prerequisites: Meta Ad Library access, read-only
steps: Search the product keyword in the Ad Library, and check each named competitor's page through Page Transparency.
Mark brands that look like they are scaling: many variations, repeated creatives, professional production.
Watch video ads and note the visible person's rough age, gender and body type, labeled as an estimate.
Note the desires and USPs the creative leans on.
Repeat across competitors until the picture is stable, then write the mainstream avatar as a who-to-avoid profile.

test.method: No paid test; this is a research step that informs which avatar to build next.

title: Clear 3 proof checks, real struggle, enough people, real want, before deep research on a new avatar
hypothesis: If we require a candidate avatar to clear 3 proof checks, struggle, size, and want, before spending on deep research, then we stop wasting effort on candidates that only look promising because they are isolated.

signal.check: A candidate avatar is about to get a deep-research pass or a creative brief without documented evidence for struggle, size and want.

prerequisites: A candidate avatar profile from review or forum mining
steps: Check struggle: turn the review's detail into a plain search on Reddit, for example post C-section weight gain Reddit, and judge thread volume and recency.
Check size: estimate how many people fit this profile.
Check want: confirm there is a desperate want for the product's actual outcome, not just isolation from the mainstream.
Log all 3 checks with evidence before the candidate moves to deep research or a creative brief.

test.method: Track how many candidates that passed all 3 checks led to a working creative test versus candidates that skipped a check.
test.read_point: After a full research and test cycle.

title: Target buyers who already paid for a failed solution as the best prospects
hypothesis: If we tag and prioritize quotes from people who already spent money on a failed solution, then copy can speak to the highest-intent buyers, the ones who believe the problem is real and are still hunting for an answer.

signal.check: Reviews, forum comments or interviews include phrases like I spent thousands and it didn't work, but these have not been tagged as a separate high-intent group.

prerequisites: Reviews or interviews mentioning a prior spend on a failed solution
steps: Search 1-star and 5-star reviews, forum comments, and interview transcripts for phrases like I spent, I tried, I already tried X and it didn't Y.
Tag every such quote as high-intent evidence.
Use these quotes to drive the failed-solution field and the belief sequence in the record.
Lean into these quotes for the hook, since these buyers already believe the problem is real.

test.method: Test a hook or ad built on a named failed-solution quote against a generic problem-first hook.

title: Split the avatar record by consequence, cohort or prior insecurity, not just by condition
hypothesis: If we split an avatar when research shows the same condition leads to different consequences, cohorts or motives, then copy can speak to the real stake instead of averaging different buyers into one record.

signal.check: Research shows the same problem described with different consequences, such as can't do my job versus can't play sports, but the avatar record treats them as one.

prerequisites: At least 2 distinct consequence or cohort quotes for the same problem
steps: Read quotes describing the same problem or condition.
Note whether the consequence, cohort, or prior insecurity differs, such as job impact versus hobby impact, or a 20-year-old versus a 50-year-old.
If they differ meaningfully, split into separate avatar records.
Tag each record with its specific consequence and cohort so copy and platform choice match.

test.method: Run separate creative for each split avatar and compare against the combined, averaged version.
test.read_point: After normal test spend for each.

title: Place a new product idea in the price by customer-count matrix before deep research
hypothesis: If we place a new product idea in a price versus number-of-customers matrix before deep research, then we can drop a labour-of-love idea early instead of spending research time on it.
does_not_apply_when: The product already exists in the catalogue with real sales data

signal.check: A new product or offer idea is about to get deep avatar research with no rough estimate of its price and customer-count quadrant.

risk.note: This is a napkin estimate, not a measurement; do not treat the quadrant as final.

prerequisites: A one-sentence description of the product idea and its likely price
steps: Estimate the likely price point of the idea.
Estimate roughly how many people could want it.
Place it in one of 4 quadrants: high price and few customers, high price and many, low price and many, or low price and few.
Discard or rework a labour-of-love idea, low price and few customers, before spending more research time.
Note which quadrant the format sits in for the priority record.

test.method: No paid test; this is a screening step before committing research hours.
test.read_point: Before starting deep research on a new idea.

title: Prefer passive struggle data over active sales data when building the avatar record
hypothesis: If the avatar record is built from passive data, what people tried, what frustrated them, what they rigged up, instead of only order and CRM fields, then it captures the cause of the purchase, not just the outcome.

signal.check: The avatar record is built only from order data, RFM fields, or platform demographics, with no ticket, review, or interview evidence.

prerequisites: Access to support tickets, return reasons, or reviews, not only order data
steps: Check what the avatar record is currently built from.
If it is only sales or CRM fields, add support tickets, return reasons, and review text.
Look specifically for what customers tried before, what frustrated them, and what they rigged up.
Reject a record for review that has no passive data source.

test.method: Compare copy or angle ideas generated from a passive-data-only record against the current active-data-only record.

title: Enter a newly forming trend through an adjacent product, not the crowded core item
hypothesis: If we serve a newly forming recreational or lifestyle trend through an adjacent product category instead of the crowded core product, then we can be first to an avatar before the mainstream players saturate it.
does_not_apply_when: The trend has no visibly growing community yet

signal.check: A recreational or lifestyle trend is visibly growing, and the core product category is already crowded with mainstream competitors.

risk.note: This is a hypothetical lever with no source-run example; treat any product decision as a separate call to product research.

prerequisites: A visibly growing trend identified through social content or search interest
steps: Identify a trend that is visibly growing but whose core product category is already crowded.
List adjacent categories, such as clothing, supplements, or drinks, that could serve the same emerging community.
Route the actual product choice to product research; use this folder only to define the avatar for that adjacent entry.
Build the avatar around the trend community's identity, not the core product's existing buyers.

test.method: Run a small test campaign for the adjacent product against the community and compare cost per result to a core-category benchmark.

title: Build a separate avatar for each price tier when the brand sells across a range
hypothesis: If a budget-tier buyer and a premium-tier buyer get separate avatar records instead of one shared record, then objections and proof can match the tier, since the two buyers likely have different worries and needs.
does_not_apply_when: The brand sells at one price point or a narrow range

signal.check: The brand sells across a wide price range but has only one avatar record covering both tiers.

risk.note: No source states this directly; verify against the brand's own price-tier sales data before use.

prerequisites: Sales data broken out by price tier or SKU
steps: Identify the brand's price tiers.
Pull reviews and interviews separately for budget-tier and premium-tier buyers.
Run the demand matrix separately for each tier instead of once for the whole catalogue.
Write a separate avatar record for each tier if objections or proof needs clearly differ.

test.method: Test tier-specific proof or objection-handling copy against the current shared copy for each tier.
test.read_point: After normal test spend per tier.

title: Anchor on marketplace reviews and Q&A when the brand has sales but no reachable customer list
hypothesis: If a marketplace-only seller anchors avatar research on marketplace reviews, Q&A, and the Ad Library instead of assuming it can interview buyers, then the avatar work fits the actual data the brand has access to.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has a first-party customer list with contact information

signal.check: The brand sells mainly through a marketplace with no CRM or first-party customer list, so there is no way to interview or survey buyers directly.

risk.note: Mark every record built this way provisional until a first-party list exists.

prerequisites: Marketplace listing access and Ad Library access
steps: Confirm the brand has sales but no first-party customer list or CRM.
Mine marketplace reviews and Q&A the same way as competitor reviews would be mined.
Run the Ad Library map as the new-market path, even though the brand has sales.
Mark every avatar record built this way provisional until a first-party list exists.
Start building a first-party list, such as a post-purchase email capture, so this branch can be retired.

test.method: Once a first-party list exists, compare the provisional marketplace-based avatar against interview findings from real buyers.
test.read_point: Once the first email or SMS list reaches interview-worthy size.

title: Run a 60-minute research sprint before writing any copy round
hypothesis: If every copy round starts with a 60-minute research sprint, 30 minutes of forums and 30 minutes of reviews, then copy is grounded in fresh quotes instead of guesses, and stalled creative gets diagnosed as a research gap early.

signal.check: A copy round is about to start with no research sprint logged in the last few weeks for this avatar.

prerequisites: A research evidence file for this brand
A starting demographic or identity from top customers or a competitor read
steps: Open the evidence file and add a dated sprint header with product, candidate avatar, and who is running it.
Spend 30 minutes in forums: search the avatar's own words plus reddit, read threads and comments, paste quotes verbatim with URL and date.
Spend 30 minutes on Amazon reviews of competing products: log fears, desired outcomes, emotional states, and failed solutions by star band.
Write the dominant emotional state with 2 or 3 supporting quotes.
List named failed solutions with cost where given, and draft a job statement as verb plus noun.
Mark the record provisional, sprint only.
Run the 30-second riff test and the 3-question check; if either fails, schedule a second sprint on a different source before writing copy.
Audit current or AI-drafted copy against the file and write a gap list for the next test round.

test.method: Compare copy written after a completed sprint against copy written without one, on the same audience.

title: Require at least 2 source types per avatar record, with 1 first-party source for an existing brand
hypothesis: If a record must cite at least 2 source types, and at least 1 first-party source for a brand with buyers, then the avatar is not built on a single unrepresentative slice of data.

signal.check: An avatar record cites only 1 source type, such as forum posts alone, with no first-party review, ticket, survey or interview.

prerequisites: Access to at least 2 different research sources, such as reviews and forums
steps: Count how many distinct source types the record currently cites.
If fewer than 2, add a second source type such as reviews, tickets, or a survey.
For a brand with existing buyers, confirm at least 1 first-party source is present, such as the brand's own reviews or an interview.
Reject the record at review if this floor is not met.

test.method: No paid test; this is a record-quality gate checked before the record is used.
test.read_point: Before the record is handed to creative or copy.

title: Read reviews by star band, since each band shows a different signal
hypothesis: If reviews are read separately by star band, 5-star for likes and identity, 3-star for structural complaints, 1-star for failure and trust breaks, then the record captures signals a single mixed read would blur together.

signal.check: Review mining has been done without separating quotes by star band.

prerequisites: Access to the brand's own reviews and the top 5 to 10 competitor or category products
steps: Sort each listing by top reviews and, where available, filter to reviews with images or video.
5-star pass: log what buyers genuinely like and every identity marker.
3-star pass, and the 2 to 4 band: log structural, recurring complaints, not one-off taste complaints.
1-star pass: log explicit failure points, physical friction, broken trust markers, and worn-out claims.
Tag every quote with its listing URL, star band, and date.

test.method: No paid test; this is a research method check on the review-mining pass.

title: Prioritize long narrative reviews over short generic ones for avatar discovery
hypothesis: If review mining focuses on long narrative reviews that tell a life story instead of short generic ones, then avatar discovery finds usable detail instead of empty praise.

signal.check: Review mining is spending time reading short reviews like works great instead of long narrative reviews.

risk.note: Short reviews still count for tallying identity markers and star-band sentiment.

prerequisites: A listing to mine with a mix of short and long reviews
steps: Skip short generic reviews for avatar discovery purposes.
Look for reviews that narrate weight history, surgery, stress, age, or physical limits.
Log each distinct life-story profile as a numbered candidate with a short identifier, never a full name.
Stop at 3 to 4 candidates for a new-avatar discovery pass.

test.method: No paid test; compare candidate quality from a long-review-only pass against a mixed pass.

title: Discount single contradictory reviews and act only on repeated complaint patterns
hypothesis: If we log contradictory single reviews without changing the avatar or copy on the spot, and only act once a pattern repeats, then the record stays stable instead of chasing one keyboard-warrior opinion.

signal.check: A single negative or contradictory review is about to trigger a change to the avatar record or copy.

prerequisites: A batch of reviews for the same product or category
steps: When 2 reviews contradict each other, log both instead of picking a side immediately.
Note whether the reviewer actually applied the product correctly before treating a complaint as a real gap.
Wait for the complaint to repeat across independent reviewers before changing the record or copy.
Where possible, find a synthesis, such as a simple main message with a technical appendix, instead of choosing 1 voice.

test.method: No paid test; track how often single-review reactions were reversed once a pattern check was added.

title: Search forums using the avatar's own words, not marketing language
hypothesis: If forum searches use the plain words a customer would actually type, such as my cat won't drink water please help reddit, instead of marketing phrasing, then the search surfaces real emotional language instead of generic content.

signal.check: Forum research is using category or marketing terms, such as cat hydration supplement market, instead of a customer's plain complaint.

prerequisites: A category subreddit or forum list for the product
steps: Adopt the avatar's mind state before searching.
Type the query the way the avatar would type it, adding reddit to the search.
Add identity qualifiers, such as men or over 30, to sharpen the search when needed.
Let the vocabulary in one thread guide the next search query.
Use condition-specific subreddits and niche groups, not general feeds.

test.method: Compare the usable quote count from a plain-language search against a marketing-language search on the same topic.

title: Read the comments on a forum thread, not only the original post
hypothesis: If forum research reads the comment replies and not only the original post, then it captures the rawest material, since confession-style communities often carry their sharpest quotes in the replies.

signal.check: Forum research entries only quote original posts, with no reply-level quotes logged.

prerequisites: A forum thread already identified as relevant
steps: Open the full thread, not just the headline post.
Read every comment, especially in confession-style communities.
Paste useful comment-level quotes into the evidence file with their own URL and date.
Spot-check a sample of past sprint entries to confirm replies were actually read.

test.method: No paid test; spot-check entries for reply-level quotes as part of the sprint check.

title: Use Reddit for emotional language and Quora for tactics, then verify per category
hypothesis: If we treat Reddit as the source for emotional mechanics and Quora as the source for tactics, but follow the content when a thread breaks that pattern, then research time goes to the platform most likely to hold the signal needed.

signal.check: Research time is split evenly between Reddit and Quora with no sense of which platform is giving emotional versus tactical content for this category.

risk.note: Both platforms have changed since this pattern was first observed in 2018; check current behavior for the category.

prerequisites: Access to both Reddit and Quora for the category
steps: Start with the category subreddit for emotional register, such as a skincare subreddit for a skincare brand.
Use the how-to subreddit or Quora for tactical, how-to language.
If a Reddit thread turns out tactical or a Quora thread turns out emotional, follow the content, not the platform label.
Note which platform actually delivered which type of content for this category, for next time.

test.method: No paid test; compare quote yield by type between the 2 platforms for this category.
test.read_point: After one research pass per platform.

title: Capture every research quote verbatim, keeping the harsh wording
hypothesis: If quotes are copied word for word instead of paraphrased or softened, then copy can reuse the exact language that actually sells, instead of a marketer's cleaned-up version of it.

signal.check: Research notes contain paraphrased or softened summaries instead of exact quotes with a source URL and date.

prerequisites: A live research evidence file
steps: Copy whole posts and comments into the evidence file exactly as written, with spacing preserved.
Bold or underline emotional language, named failed solutions, situational detail, and self-descriptions.
Use a screenshot when a post is dense, rather than summarizing it.
Keep harsh wording exactly as written; do not soften or script it.
Do not summarize with an AI tool at this capture stage.

test.method: Spot-check 5 evidence entries against their source URLs for exact wording.

title: Name the avatar's single dominant emotional state and set the copy register from it
hypothesis: If each avatar record names one dominant emotional state, frustration, fear, anxiety, guilt, embarrassment or shame, with 2 or 3 quotes, then the copy register matches the real emotional tone instead of guessing.

signal.check: The avatar record has no stated dominant emotion, or lists several with no clear lead.

prerequisites: At least 2 or 3 quotes showing an emotional reaction to the problem
steps: Read the quotes collected for this avatar.
Pick the single most repeated emotional state, such as frustration or fear.
Attach 2 or 3 quotes that show this state.
If 2 states split the evidence roughly evenly, consider splitting into 2 avatars instead of picking one.

test.method: Test copy written in the named emotional register against copy written in a generic or wrong register.

title: Track repeated words and unexpected benefit links across research batches
hypothesis: If we track words that keep recurring across research threads and note any counterintuitive benefit link, then copy can use a benefit connection customers already make instead of one the brand invents.

signal.check: A word or phrase keeps showing up across different threads or reviews, but no one has run a follow-up search on it.

prerequisites: A batch of forum or review quotes already collected
steps: After each research batch, list words that repeated 3 or more times.
Run a follow-up search on any recurring word to see where it leads.
Write down any unexpected benefit link, such as weight loss connecting to feeling more respected.
Tag which sub-avatar feels each unexpected link most strongly.

test.method: Test a benefit angle built on a counterintuitive link against the brand's current default benefit angle.

title: Mine Google autocomplete and Keyword Planner for what people say they want
hypothesis: If we log Google autocomplete suggestions and Keyword Planner volumes for the niche, then PDP titles, meta descriptions and ad headlines can use language people actually type, sized by real search volume.

signal.check: PDP titles, meta descriptions or ad headlines are written without checking autocomplete or keyword volume for the target country.

risk.note: Search volume is an input for language, not a mandate to buy or build.

prerequisites: Google Ads Keyword Planner access, read-only
steps: Type the niche keyword into Google without pressing enter and record every relevant suggestion.
Type a promising suggestion as the next stem and record the next layer, repeating 2 to 3 times.
Use Keyword Planner's discover new keywords flow for the target countries, reading volume, competition and seasonality.
Use the language found for PDP titles, meta descriptions and ad headlines, treating volume as an input, not proof of buying intent.

test.method: Test a PDP title or ad headline built from autocomplete language against the current title.
test.read_point: After a few weeks of indexed traffic or normal ad test spend.

title: Cross-check Google search interest against Amazon buying behavior before weighting a benefit
hypothesis: If we compare what people search for on Google against what they actually buy on Amazon, and weight Amazon more for offer and product decisions, then the record separates stated want from real buying behavior instead of treating search interest as proof.

signal.check: Google search interest for a benefit or angle is high, but no one has checked whether Amazon buying behavior actually supports it, or the reverse.

risk.note: Review counts are a rough sales proxy, explicitly a guess.

prerequisites: Access to Google search volume and Amazon listings for the category
steps: Type the keyword into Amazon and record autocomplete suggestions.
Read book titles and subtitles, or the most optimized listings, as pre-tested language.
Open listings and read reviews for likes and dislikes.
Compare the Google dataset (stated want) against the Amazon dataset (actual buying).
Where they disagree, weight Amazon for offer and product decisions, and Google for messaging language.
Note the gap in the record rather than picking one dataset and ignoring the mismatch.

test.method: Test an offer or product claim weighted by the Amazon-favored benefit against one weighted by the Google-favored benefit.

title: Use Meta Ad Library ad duration as a screening signal, never as proof of a winning angle
hypothesis: If a long-running competitor ad is treated only as a screen to corroborate with reviews and keyword demand, not as proof of a winning angle, then the team avoids copying an angle that just happens to still be running.

signal.check: A long-running competitor ad is being adopted as an angle without checking it against review or keyword evidence.

expected_effect.size: unknown, explicitly hedged by the source as not always true

risk.note: Never copy the ad's text, images, or offer; adapt the angle only.

prerequisites: Meta Ad Library access, read-only
steps: Search the product keyword and named competitors in the Ad Library, or use Page Transparency to reach a competitor's ads.
Note ads that recur across a scan and ads that appear lowest in the feed, since these are running longest.
Corroborate any long-running angle against review and keyword demand before adopting it.
Adapt the angle in your own words; never copy the text, image or offer.

test.method: Test the adapted angle against the brand's current best-performing angle.

title: Read competitor headlines for the constraint and reward they encode
hypothesis: If we read competitor headlines specifically for the constraint and reward they encode, such as time-poor or challenge-seeking, then the record captures sub-market clues a plain feature comparison would miss.

signal.check: Competitor sites and headlines have not been reviewed for the specific buyer constraint and reward each one is aimed at.

risk.note: Named competitor characterizations may be stale; re-check before reuse.

prerequisites: A list of the category's competitor sites
steps: For each competitor site, read the imagery, tone and headline.
Name the sub-market each one speaks to, based on its own distinctions.
Read each headline for the constraint and reward it encodes, such as an hour's worth of results in 25 minutes signaling a time-poor buyer.
Judge overall polish: do competitors look like real businesses, or is the whole field amateur?
Log format, price and matrix quadrant for each site.

test.method: No paid test; this feeds sub-market candidates into the priority list.
test.read_point: Before finalizing avatar candidates for a new market.

title: Search social content for category terms to map mass, niche and sub-avatar layers
hypothesis: If we search broad category terms on the brand's social platforms and trace the mass, niche and sub-avatar layers, then we can pick a sub-avatar the brand can signal consistently across creative, product and language.

signal.check: The category has visible social communities but no one has mapped how they split into layers or sub-avatars.

risk.note: Characterizations of named brands are the agent's own reading; re-check before reuse.

prerequisites: Access to the platform where the category is most visible, such as TikTok
steps: Search broad category terms on the platform, such as gym clothing or CrossFit.
Note the distinct groups posting and what visibly separates them.
Trace the nesting: mass layer, niche layer, sub-avatar layer, and the next unserved slice.
Log each brand's identity signals: creative style, product design, language, and who it uplifts.
Pick a sub-avatar the brand can signal consistently across all of those at once.

test.method: No paid test; use the mapped sub-avatar as an input to the priority list.
test.read_point: Before finalizing which sub-avatar to pursue.

title: Confirm where the avatar spends time with platform demographic data, not a guess
hypothesis: If every record's Where field cites actual platform demographic data instead of an assumed cohort-to-platform map, then media placement and phrasing match where the avatar actually is, avoiding a mismatch like TikTok phrasing aimed at a 50-plus audience.

signal.check: The avatar record's Where field is a guess, such as assuming older buyers only use Facebook, with no platform demographic data behind it.

prerequisites: Access to platform demographic data for the brand's countries
steps: Search current platform demographics for the brand's target countries.
Check the avatar's profile against each platform's actual skew.
Pull phrasing from where that cohort actually posts, not from a platform the team assumes they use.
Cite the data source in the record's Where field.

test.method: Test the same creative concept on the confirmed platform against the previously assumed platform.
test.read_point: After normal ad test spend on each platform.

title: Use digital intelligence and social listening tools to check interview themes against the wider audience
hypothesis: If we run a digital intelligence or social listening tool on the wider category audience and compare it against interview themes, then we catch a mismatch between what a small interviewed sample says and what the broader audience actually talks about.

signal.check: Avatar themes come only from a small interviewed sample, with no check against the wider audience's public conversation.

risk.note: Confirm current availability and pricing of any named tool before relying on it.

prerequisites: Access to a social listening or digital intelligence tool
steps: Use a tool such as SparkToro or a similar platform-usage tool to see which platforms and influencers the wider audience follows.
Use a social listening tool to track the category's topics, pains and frustrations in people's own words, not brand mentions.
Run this on the wider audience, separate from the interviewed sample.
Compare the results with interview themes and log matches and mismatches.

test.method: No paid test; this is a cross-check step before finalizing the record's themes.

title: Run real customer interviews instead of relying only on online research
hypothesis: If the brand runs real interviews with confirmed buyers instead of relying only on online strangers, then the record captures the why behind behavior, since online answers cannot be verified and people say what they think others want to hear.
does_not_apply_when: The brand truly has no reachable buyers yet; mark the record provisional instead

signal.check: The avatar record is built only from public online sources with no interview conducted with a confirmed buyer.

prerequisites: A customer list to filter interview invites to confirmed buyers
steps: Use the store's own order data to confirm interview candidates are real, paying buyers.
Schedule a small number of rich interviews rather than relying on a large number of shallow online data points.
Use quantitative follow-up, such as a survey, to confirm how common a theme is once interviews find it.
Mark any record with no interviews yet as provisional.

test.method: Compare copy or angle ideas sourced from interviews against ideas sourced only from online research on the same avatar.
test.read_point: After the first round of interviews.

title: Check platform, language and payment habits for the brand's real market before reusing a US read
hypothesis: If we check the brand's actual country's platform, language and payment habits instead of assuming Reddit, English and card payment apply everywhere, then research and offer decisions fit a mobile-first or non-US market instead of a US default.
does_not_apply_when: The brand's whole market is US-based and English-language

signal.check: Research or offer decisions assume Reddit, English-language forums, or card payment, but the brand's real market is mobile-first, non-English, or cash-on-delivery heavy.

risk.note: No library source; verify against the brand's own data before use.

prerequisites: Basic knowledge of the brand's target country and its dominant platforms and payment methods
steps: Identify the brand's actual target country or countries.
Check which platforms (WhatsApp, regional apps) and languages that market actually uses, instead of assuming Reddit and English.
Check payment habits, such as cash-on-delivery preference, for that market.
Adjust research sources and offer design (payment options, language) to match, instead of copying a US-only playbook.

test.method: Test a localized research and offer approach against the US-default approach in the same market.
test.read_point: After normal test spend in that market.

title: Run the full research sequence before launching a product into a new market with no customers
hypothesis: If a new product or new market runs the full research sequence, demand matrix, competitor scan, forum and Quora mining, Google and Amazon intent, Ad Library map, before writing copy, then the launch avatar is built on several source types instead of a guess.
does_not_apply_when: The brand already has real buyers for this product

signal.check: A new product or new-market launch is being planned with no structured research sequence run yet.

risk.note: A category with no repeated language pattern may lack a real struggle worth building a full record around; report that instead of inventing one.

prerequisites: A one-sentence idea naming a specific avatar
Confirmation the product has cleared product-research gates
steps: Place the idea in the price by customer-count matrix and discard a labour-of-love quadrant.
Google natural-language problem phrases and log every notable competitor site found.
For each competitor site, read imagery, tone, headline, format, price and polish.
Identify the top 5 to 10 books or products on Amazon and run the star-band review mining pass on them.
Search forums and Quora for emotional mechanics and tactical checks, tracking recurring words.
Run the Google and Amazon intent pass for stated want versus actual buying.
Run the Ad Library map for the mainstream avatar.
Schedule at least 1 real conversation with someone who fits, and compile sub-avatars with quoted pains, hopes and obstacles.

test.method: Track whether launch creative built from this sequence needs fewer rounds to find a working angle than a launch built without it.
test.read_point: After the first launch test round.

title: Use a lightweight email or DM reply as a research conversation when a call is not possible
hypothesis: If we turn a real inbound email or DM into a short research conversation with 2 or 3 lateral questions, then the brand gets first-party evidence even in weeks when a full interview cannot be scheduled.

signal.check: An inbound customer email or DM is being answered with only a support reply, and no one is using it as a research moment.

prerequisites: A real inbound customer email or DM
steps: Reply to a real inbound email or DM as normal.
Add 2 or 3 lateral questions, such as have you thought about X, or what surprised you.
Ask about day-to-day limits related to the problem.
Log the thread verbatim in the evidence file with consent status noted.
Aim for at least 1 such conversation per week.

test.method: No paid test; track how many usable quotes come from this channel per month.

title: Choose review mining or forum mining first based on the research goal, not a fixed ratio
hypothesis: If we choose whether to start with Amazon reviews or forum threads based on the actual goal, candidate discovery favors reviews, emotional register favors forums, instead of a fixed 80/20 or 50/50 split, then the sprint spends its limited time where it is most likely to pay off.

signal.check: A research sprint is following a fixed time split between reviews and forums with no thought to which goal, finding new candidates or capturing register, is more urgent right now.

risk.note: Do not cite a fixed 80/20 split as a rule; it is one presenter's own estimate of his time, not a demonstrated ratio.

prerequisites: A clear research goal for this sprint: finding new candidates, or capturing register and vocabulary
steps: Before starting, decide whether this sprint's goal is finding new avatar candidates or capturing emotional register and vocabulary.
If finding candidates, start with long Amazon reviews, since they carry life stories.
If capturing register, start with forums, since they carry confession-style language.
Still run 30 minutes on each within the sprint, just choose the order by goal.

test.method: No paid test; compare candidate or quote yield when order matches the stated goal versus when it does not.
test.read_point: After a few sprints run each way.

title: Complete one manual research sprint before running AI deep research on a new brand or category
hypothesis: If an operator completes at least 1 manual research sprint before running AI deep research for a new brand or category, then they can judge the AI output instead of mistaking polished text for real understanding.
does_not_apply_when: A manual sprint has already been completed for this brand and category

signal.check: AI deep research is about to run as the first and only research step for a brand or category with no manual sprint done yet.

risk.note: Blind AI research before reading real reviews and tickets risks polished but false-confidence output.

prerequisites: None beyond the brand's basic product and review access
steps: Run the 60-minute manual research sprint for this brand and category first.
Read the raw reviews and forum threads yourself before opening any AI tool.
Only after the manual sprint, use AI research to accelerate or extend, not to replace, the manual read.
Use the manual quotes collected as the check on anything the AI produces.

test.method: Compare the quote-verification failure rate of AI research run before versus after a manual sprint.
test.read_point: After the first AI research run for a new brand.

title: Run an AI deep-research report on 1 prioritized candidate and verify every quote at its source
hypothesis: If an AI deep-research report is run with a fixed prompt on 1 candidate and every quote is opened and confirmed at its cited source before use, then the report speeds up research without introducing invented quotes.

signal.check: A candidate has cleared the proof checks and a manual sprint is already done, but no deep-research report has been run yet, or a past report's quotes were never verified.

risk.note: A report whose citations do not resolve is discarded and the candidate returns to forum mining.

prerequisites: At least 1 manual sprint completed for this brand and category
The candidate has cleared the 3 proof checks
steps: Open a fresh ChatGPT or Gemini session and enable deep research.
Paste a fixed template prompt, changing only the avatar field: identifier, preliminary profile, and problem in their own words.
Confirm the prompt asks for demographics, synopsis, struggles, feelings, own words, failed solutions, and beliefs.
Read the whole report, then open every cited source page.
Copy into the evidence file only quotes actually found on the cited page, with URL and date; discard the rest.
Mark the resulting record provisional, AI-assisted, verified quotes only.

test.method: Track the share of quotes from the report that failed verification at their cited source.

title: Let an LLM draft the avatar record from first-party transcripts, then verify every claim
hypothesis: If an LLM synthesizes 5 or more of the brand's own transcripts, surveys and order data into a draft avatar record, and every claim is checked against the raw transcript before it counts, then the record gets built faster without losing traceability.

signal.check: The brand has 5 or more first-party transcripts, surveys or CRM notes sitting unused because building a record from them by hand feels too slow.

risk.note: The model may not add typical quotes; every claim must cite a transcript id.

prerequisites: 5 or more first-party transcripts, survey results, or CRM notes for this brand
steps: Create a dedicated project or knowledge base in Claude or ChatGPT, kept to 1 brand only.
Load call transcripts, survey results, order data summary, and product and pricing info.
Ask who am I speaking to, what pains recur, what themes repeat, what words do they use, citing the transcript id for each claim.
Ask it to draft the record fields from the inputs only, marking any field it cannot support.
Review every claim against the raw transcripts and replace any paraphrased quote with the verbatim line.

test.method: Track how many draft claims survived the raw-transcript check unchanged versus how many needed a fix or removal.

title: Build a live LLM persona from the confirmed record for directional QA questions, never for new quotes
hypothesis: If the team loads a confirmed avatar record and its evidence into a project and asks directional questions before each brief, then new hires and copy rounds get a quick sanity check without inventing new customer language.

signal.check: Every campaign or brief is checked against the avatar record by memory instead of a queryable tool, or a new team member has no fast way to learn the avatar.

risk.note: If the project ever invents a quote, tighten the instruction and re-run; it must say no evidence when there is none.

prerequisites: A confirmed avatar record with its evidence file
steps: Load only the record and its evidence file into a project, instructed to answer with quote ids or say no evidence.
Before each brief or copy round, ask directional questions: would this resonate, what would she push back on, what proof is missing.
Treat every answer as a hypothesis to check against real quotes before it enters copy.
Use the same project to brief new team members on the avatar.

test.method: Track whether briefs that used the persona project needed fewer research questions answered manually.

title: Match content altitude, beginner or advanced, to each avatar's actual experience level
hypothesis: If PDP copy and email content are pitched at the avatar's real experience level with the category, novice or expert, instead of one default level for everyone, then the content lands instead of feeling too basic or too advanced.

signal.check: The same content altitude is used for a first-time buyer's PDP and a repeat buyer's retention email, with no note of the avatar's experience level.

risk.note: Covering both altitudes is fine; the mistake is not deciding which one a given piece of content is for.

prerequisites: An avatar record noting experience level with the category
steps: Record the avatar's experience level with the category as a field: novice or expert.
Write PDP copy at a beginner level for a novice avatar.
Write retention emails at a more advanced level for a repeat, experienced buyer.
Feed the model audience context plus past content performance so the altitude call is grounded, not guessed.

test.method: Test a beginner-level PDP line against an advanced-level one on the same novice-avatar traffic.

title: Reject any avatar draft missing a quote set, a trigger moment, or a job statement
hypothesis: If no avatar record leaves the research stage without quoted evidence, a trigger moment, and a job statement, then no demographic-only draft gets used for copy or creative.

signal.check: A draft avatar record is being handed to creative or copy without all 3 of quoted evidence, a trigger moment, and a job statement.

prerequisites: A draft avatar record
steps: Check the draft for 3 to 5 minimum quotes with source ids.
Check for 1 trigger moment written as a datable event with its quote.
Check for a job statement that passed the verb-noun and cross-category tests.
Reject and send back to research any draft missing one of these 3.

test.method: No paid test; this is a record-quality gate applied before handoff.

title: Trace every quote to its real source and strip full reviewer names before it enters a record
hypothesis: If every quote carries its URL or record id, date, and source type, and reviewer identities are cut down to a short identifier, then the record stays honest and safe to share without exposing anyone's identity.

signal.check: A quote in the record has no URL, record id, or date, or a reviewer's full name is stored instead of a short identifier.

risk.note: If a quote has no traceable source, remove it and mark the field no evidence instead of guessing.

prerequisites: An evidence file already collecting quotes
steps: Spot-check every quote for a URL or record id, a date, and a source type.
Remove any quote with no traceable source; mark the field no evidence if that empties it.
Replace any full reviewer name with a short identifier, such as Anna Z, not the full name or other identifying detail.
For interview quotes, log the interview id, consent status, and whether the customer allowed quotation in marketing.

test.method: No paid test; this is a compliance and quality gate checked before the record is used.

title: Assemble the complete avatar record with every field, or mark it no evidence yet
hypothesis: If every field in the full avatar record template gets filled from real evidence or explicitly marked no evidence yet, then creative and copy get a complete, honest picture instead of a record with silent gaps.

signal.check: An avatar record is missing several of the standard fields (identity, struggles, beliefs, 5W, job spec, not-for line) with no note on why.

risk.note: A record that fails review goes back to research, not to the copywriter.

prerequisites: An evidence file with at least 2 source types
A validated job statement
steps: Fill identity and demographics as context only, day-to-day struggles, dominant emotion, and own words verbatim.
Fill failed past solutions by name and cost, limiting beliefs, and beliefs about competitors.
Write the 3 required elements at the top: quotes, trigger moment, job statement.
Write the 4 forces with a quote each, and what was fired.
Write miracles and miseries as 2 specific lists, and the why chain per benefit.
Write the job spec: tradeoffs, full competitive set including do-nothing, and obstacles paired with removers or untested.
Write consequence segment, cohort, platform habits, experience level, and the not-for line.
Set status: provisional, confirmed, or validated, and run the record review checklist before handoff.

test.method: Compare conversion or editing effort on copy built from a complete record against copy built from a partial one.

title: Write a not-for line saying who the product is wrong for
hypothesis: If every avatar record and page carries a not-for line, then wrong-fit buyers self-select out before purchase, reducing bad-fit returns and 1-star reviews.

signal.check: The record and product page have no line telling a wrong-fit visitor this product is not for them.

prerequisites: Reviews or return reasons showing a wrong-fit use case
steps: Read 1-star reviews and return reasons for signs of a wrong-fit buyer.
Write a not-for line naming who this product will not satisfy.
Add the line to the avatar record and hand it to the landing page team to place on the product page.
Curate reviews shown on the page by use case so wrong-fit visitors can self-select out.

test.method: Track return rate and 1-star review rate for the SKU before and after adding the not-for line to the page.

title: Write miracles and miseries as specific, quoted lists, not generic wish statements
hypothesis: If the miracles (wants, dreams, goals) and miseries (fears, frustrations, pains) lists are written from quotes instead of generic phrases like wants better quality, then they give copy something concrete to promise or agitate.

signal.check: The record's miracles or miseries lists contain generic phrases with no supporting quote.

prerequisites: A batch of reviews or interview quotes
steps: Read through collected quotes for wants, dreams, goals, and desires; list them as miracles.
Read through collected quotes for fears, frustrations, pains, and problems; list them as miseries.
Replace any generic item, such as wants better quality, with the specific quoted version.
Cross-check both lists against what reviews actually said.

test.method: Test a hook or promise built from a specific miracle-list item against a generic version.

title: Chain each benefit to the personal reason it matters, and check it fits this offer
hypothesis: If each benefit is chained from feature to personal motivation, such as faster charging leads to less morning stress leads to not late for school drop-off, then the strongest chain can lead the copy instead of a generic feature list.

signal.check: The record lists benefits with no chain to a personal motivation, or the lead benefit was picked without comparing chain strength.

risk.note: Check the avatar actually benefits from this specific offer, not just the category in general.

prerequisites: A list of product features or benefits
steps: For each feature, write the functional benefit it produces.
Chain that benefit to a personal motivation, in the avatar's own words where possible.
Rank benefits by how strong and well-quoted the chain is.
Lead copy with the benefit whose chain is strongest for this avatar.

test.method: Test copy leading with the strongest-chain benefit against copy leading with the current default benefit.

title: Audit which briefs cited each avatar record every quarter, and retire the ones nobody uses
hypothesis: If the team tracks which briefs, ads and emails cited each avatar record and retires or revises the ones cited by nothing, then avatar work stops piling up as unused documents nobody reopens.

signal.check: The brand has avatar records but no log of which briefs or campaigns actually used them, and it has been a quarter or more since the last check.

expected_effect.size: unknown, 1 cited source found about 90% of marketers create personas and 77% never use them

prerequisites: A log or ability to check which brief cited which avatar record
steps: List the quarter's briefs, launches, and copy rounds.
For each, note which avatar record, if any, it cited.
For records cited by nothing, ask the team why: wrong fields, not findable, not trusted.
Revise, merge, or retire unused records, and keep whatever label the team already uses for the deliverable.
Distribute the revised record to marketing, product, support and sales.

test.method: Track the persona usage rate, the share of briefs citing a record by name, quarter over quarter.

title: Block any sensitive-attribute assertion about the viewer before a creative handoff
hypothesis: If every creative brief is checked for lines that assert a viewer's health, body, age, finances, or protected attribute as fact, and those lines are rephrased as quoted stories instead, then the brand avoids breaching Meta's advertising policy on personal attributes.

signal.check: A creative brief or hook states or implies a fact about the viewer's health, body, age, money, or protected status, such as you have X condition.

risk.note: A policy breach can get ads disapproved or the ad account flagged; check current Meta advertising standards before every handoff.

prerequisites: Current Meta advertising standards on personal attributes and personal health
steps: Read every line of the brief as if it were live ad copy.
Flag any line that asserts a viewer's health, body, age, financial state, or protected attribute as a fact about them.
Rewrite the situation as a quoted forum line or story the creative may echo, instead of a direct assertion.
If a line cannot be rephrased without the assertion, drop the angle rather than ship it.
Check current Meta policy on personal attributes before every handoff, since it can change.

test.method: No paid test; this is a compliance gate checked before every creative handoff.
test.read_point: Before every creative or copy handoff.

title: Mark a first-pass sketch built only from ads and reviews as provisional, not a finished avatar
hypothesis: If a bare-bones sketch built only from ads, reviews and forum reads is labeled provisional instead of treated as a finished avatar, then the team knows to keep validating it with real buyers before betting a scale attempt on it.

signal.check: A profile built from a first sprint or public data alone is being used to plan a scale attempt as if it were fully confirmed.

prerequisites: A first-pass avatar sketch
steps: Check the record's evidence: is it only public data (ads, reviews, forums) with no first-party confirmation?
If so, mark the record provisional and note it is enough to audit copy against, not to plan a scale attempt.
For a brand with buyers, upgrade the status once real buyers confirm it through interviews.
For a brand with no buyers, upgrade only after the deep-research report is verified and the first real buyers are interviewed.

test.method: No paid test; this is a status label check before any scale decision is made.

title: Add a size or fit-confidence angle whenever an avatar's anxieties include sizing or fit
hypothesis: If the angle map adds a size-guide or fit-confidence angle whenever the record's anxieties include sizing or fit, then copy and page proof can directly address a known return driver instead of leaving it unaddressed.
does_not_apply_when: The product has no size or fit variable at all

signal.check: The avatar record lists sizing or fit as an anxiety, but the angle map has no dedicated size or fit-confidence angle.

prerequisites: An avatar record with sizing or fit named as an anxiety
steps: Check the record's anxieties field for any mention of sizing or fit.
If present, add a size-guide or fit-confidence angle to the angle map.
Pair the angle with the best available proof, such as a size chart, a fit quiz, or fit-specific reviews.
Hand the angle to the page and creative teams alongside the other angles.

test.method: Track return rate for fit-related reasons before and after the size or fit-confidence angle ships on the page.

title: Check the avatar's synopsis names a real circumstance, not just age, gender and income
